meta.author: bank-team-integrated-1
meta.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.topic: Simple interest compared with compound interest
questions.learningObjective: Compare simple and compound interest over one period
questions.stem: Ticket T-001 asks whether simple interest grows faster than compound interest at the same nominal rate over one period.

options.text: For one period both give the same total interest.
Compound interest grows faster once compounding begins.
options.misconception: ignores that simple interest can match in first period

options.text: Simple interest always grows faster because it avoids fees.
options.misconception: confuses absence of compounding with faster growth

options.text: Neither earns interest because rates cancel.

questions.explanation: In the first period simple and compound interest agree; compounding only adds extra later, so the tempting claim that one always dominates fails.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how compounding frequency affects balance
questions.stem: Ticket T-002 claims monthly compounding leaves the same balance as annual compounding at the same nominal rate.

options.text: Monthly compounding always leaves a lower balance than annual compounding.
Monthly compounding leaves a higher balance than annual compounding.
Frequency does not matter because the nominal rate is fixed.
Only the principal matters when rates are equal.

questions.explanation: More frequent compounding earns interest on interest sooner, so the monthly balance exceeds the annual one; the error is treating frequency as irrelevant.

questions.stem: Ticket T-003 asks a teammate to explain why a 50 percent markup is not a 50 percent margin.

answer.exemplar: Markup is profit divided by cost, while margin is profit divided by selling price; a 50 percent markup on cost gives a selling price of 1.5 times cost, so margin is one third, not one half, because the base differs.

questions.explanation: The two ratios use different bases, so equal percentages cannot describe the same profit; the wrong idea treats markup and margin as interchangeable.
questions.hint: Check the denominator of each ratio.

questions.learningObjective: Compute a tax-added price from a base
questions.stem: Ticket T-004 needs the total when a 100 price has 8 percent tax added on top.
questions.explanation: Tax added means multiply the base by 1.08, giving 108; the tempting error is treating the total as already tax inclusive.
questions.hint: Multiply by one plus the rate.

questions.learningObjective: Find the better package by unit price
questions.stem: Ticket T-005 compares 3 for 5.00 against 5 for 8.00 and wants the cheaper unit price.
questions.explanation: The first package costs about 1.67 per item and the second 1.60, so the larger package is cheaper; the wrong choice picks the lower total.

questions.topic: Annual percentage rate against note rate
questions.learningObjective: Explain why APR exceeds note rate
questions.stem: Ticket T-006 asks why the annual percentage rate on a loan is higher than the stated note rate.

options.text: APR is always lower because lenders discount it.
options.misconception: assumes APR is a discounted rate

options.text: APR is just the note rate rounded to two decimals.
APR excludes all charges except pure interest.
APR adds fees and points to the interest cost.

questions.explanation: APR folds fees and points into the annual cost, so it exceeds the note rate; the error is treating APR as a simple rounded rate.
questions.hint: Include fees in the annual cost.

questions.learningObjective: State what a market index measures
questions.stem: Ticket T-007 asks what a broad market index is designed to measure.

options.text: The profit of one randomly chosen company.
The performance of a representative basket of securities.
The total cash in every bank account.
The exchange rate of one currency pair.

questions.explanation: An index tracks a basket to represent a market; the wrong ideas confuse it with a single stock, money supply, or currency pair.

questions.learningObjective: Compute real return from nominal and inflation
questions.stem: Ticket T-008 says a 5 percent nominal return with 2 percent inflation gives a 7 percent real return.

options.text: Real return is 5 percent because inflation is ignored.
Real return is 7 percent because rates add.
Real return is about 3 percent, not 7 percent.
Real return is 2 percent because nominal is ignored.

questions.explanation: Real return subtracts inflation from nominal, so about 3 percent; the error adds the two rates instead of subtracting.

questions.learningObjective: Solve break-even from cost and revenue
questions.stem: Ticket T-009 asks how to find the break-even quantity from linear cost and revenue functions.

answer.exemplar: Set total cost equal to total revenue, solve for quantity, and check that the result is nonnegative; the wrong method stops at cost equals zero and ignores revenue.

questions.explanation: Break-even occurs where cost equals revenue, not where cost vanishes; solving the equality yields the quantity and rejects the zero-cost shortcut.

questions.topic: Budget constraint and the affordable set
questions.learningObjective: Identify affordable bundles on a budget line
questions.stem: Ticket T-010 has income 200 and prices 4 and 5; find the maximum of good X when no Y is bought.
questions.explanation: With all income spent on X, divide 200 by 4 to get 50; the tempting error divides by the price of Y.

questions.topic: Minimum payment and a revolving balance
questions.stem: Ticket T-011 estimates interest on a 1000 balance at 2 percent monthly for one month.
questions.explanation: Monthly interest is 1000 times 0.02, giving 20; the error uses the annual rate without dividing by twelve.

questions.stem: Ticket T-012 asks how a prepayment penalty is usually computed.

options.text: As the original principal amount.
As a fixed fee unrelated to balance.
As the total interest ever paid.
As a percentage of the remaining balance.

questions.explanation: Prepayment penalties are typically a percentage of the remaining balance; the wrong ideas use flat fees, total interest, or original principal.

questions.topic: Tax treatment of a retirement account
questions.learningObjective: Compare tax timing of retirement accounts
questions.stem: Ticket T-013 asks when taxes are paid in a traditional retirement account.

options.text: Contributions are taxed now and withdrawals are tax free.
Contributions reduce taxable income now and withdrawals are taxed later.
No taxes are ever paid on either side.
options.misconception: assumes tax free growth and withdrawal

options.text: Taxes are paid twice on the same money.

questions.explanation: Traditional accounts defer tax to withdrawal; the error reverses the timing or assumes no tax at all.

questions.learningObjective: Apply a discount to the correct base
questions.stem: Ticket T-014 applies a 20 percent discount to a 50 price and claims the result is 30.

options.text: The discounted price is 50 because discounts do not reduce price.
The discounted price is 30 because 50 minus 20.
The discounted price is 40, not 30.
The discounted price is 10 because 20 percent of 50 is 10.
options.misconception: confuses discount amount with final price

questions.explanation: A 20 percent discount on 50 removes 10, leaving 40; the error subtracts 20 percentage points from the price.

questions.stem: Ticket T-015 asks what it means when an exchange rate rises from 1.10 to 1.20 units of foreign currency per home currency.

answer.exemplar: A rise means the home currency buys more foreign currency, so it has strengthened; the wrong reading treats a higher number as a weaker home currency.

questions.explanation: The rate is foreign per home, so a higher value strengthens the home currency; the error reads the number as home per foreign.
questions.hint: Check which currency is the base.

questions.stem: Ticket T-016 has 100 today and prices rise 4 percent; find the equivalent purchasing power next year.
questions.explanation: Divide 100 by 1.04 to get about 96.15; the tempting error subtracts 4 from 100 directly.

questions.stem: Ticket T-017 computes simple interest on 500 at 6 percent for 3 years.
questions.explanation: Interest equals 500 times 0.06 times 3, giving 90; the error compounds the interest.
questions.hint: Use I equals P r t.

questions.topic: Solving for time under simple interest
questions.learningObjective: Solve for time in simple interest
questions.stem: Ticket T-018 asks how to solve for time when principal, rate, and interest are known.

options.text: Subtract rate from interest and principal.
Multiply interest by principal and rate.
Divide principal by interest and rate.
Divide interest by the product of principal and rate.

questions.explanation: From I equals P r t, time equals I divided by P r; the wrong steps multiply or use the wrong numerator.
questions.hint: Rearrange I equals P r t.

questions.stem: Ticket T-019 asks which formula gives the amount after annual compounding.

options.text: A equals P plus r times n.
A equals P times (1 plus r) to the n.
A equals P times r to the n.
A equals P divided by (1 plus r) to the n.

questions.explanation: Annual compounding multiplies principal by (1+r)^n; the wrong formulas use simple interest, omit the base, or discount.
questions.hint: Raise (1+r) to the number of years.

questions.topic: Effective annual rate from monthly compounding
questions.stem: Ticket T-020 says the effective annual rate for 12 percent compounded monthly is 12 percent.

options.text: The effective rate is 1 percent because 12 divided by 12.
The effective rate is 12 percent because nominal equals effective.
The effective rate is about 12.68 percent, not 12 percent.
The effective rate is 144 percent because 12 times 12.

questions.explanation: EAR is (1+r/12)^12 minus 1, about 12.68 percent; the error equates nominal and effective rates.

questions.topic: Compounding frequency and the extra amount
questions.stem: Ticket T-021 asks why more frequent compounding yields a larger final balance at the same nominal rate.

answer.exemplar: More frequent compounding applies interest to accumulated interest sooner, so the balance grows faster; the wrong view assumes frequency only changes payment timing.

questions.explanation: Earlier compounding earns interest on interest, raising the final balance; the error treats frequency as a timing detail only.

questions.topic: Level payment on an amortised loan
questions.stem: Ticket T-022 needs the level payment for 1000 at 10 percent over 2 years with annual payments.
questions.explanation: Use the annuity payment formula, giving about 576.19; the error divides principal by years and ignores interest.

questions.topic: Balance after a stated number of payments
questions.stem: Ticket T-023 asks for the balance after one payment on a 1000 loan at 10 percent over 2 years.
questions.explanation: After paying 576.19, interest is 100 and principal 476.19, leaving 523.81; the error subtracts the whole payment from principal.

questions.topic: Present value of a payment stream
questions.stem: Ticket T-024 asks which formula gives the present value of equal annual payments.

options.text: PV equals payment divided by r only.
PV equals payment times n divided by (1+r).
PV equals payment times (1+r)^n divided by r.
PV equals payment times (1 minus (1+r)^-n) divided by r.

questions.explanation: The annuity present value formula discounts each payment; the wrong forms average, compound, or ignore n.

questions.topic: Lump sum against a payment stream
questions.stem: Ticket T-025 asks which is worth more today: a lump sum or an equal payment stream with the same total nominal amount.

options.text: The payment stream is worth more because it totals more.
The lump sum is worth more because payments are delayed.
They are always equal because totals match.
options.misconception: equates nominal totals with present value

options.text: Neither has value because money loses value.

questions.explanation: Earlier money is worth more, so the lump sum wins; the error equates nominal totals with present value.

questions.stem: Ticket T-026 says a 108 total with 8 percent tax means the original price was 100 by subtracting 8.

options.text: The original price is 108 because tax is included.
The original price is 100 because 108 minus 8.
The original price is 100, but only by dividing 108 by 1.08.
The original price is 92 because 108 minus 16.

questions.explanation: To recover the base divide by 1.08, giving 100; subtracting 8 percentage points is invalid.

questions.stem: Ticket T-027 asks for the final price after a 50 percent markup then a 50 percent discount on a 100 cost.

answer.exemplar: Markup gives 150, then a 50 percent discount gives 75; the wrong idea says the two percentages cancel and the price returns to 100.

questions.explanation: Markup and discount apply to different bases, so they do not cancel; the final price is 75, not 100.

questions.learningObjective: Add sales tax to a price
questions.stem: Ticket T-028 adds 7 percent sales tax to a 200 purchase.
questions.explanation: 200 times 1.07 equals 214; the error adds 7 to 200 as dollars.

questions.topic: Tax already contained in a total
questions.stem: Ticket T-029 has a 107 total that already includes 7 percent tax; find the pre-tax price.
questions.explanation: Divide 107 by 1.07 to get 100; the error subtracts 7 percent of 107.

questions.stem: Ticket T-030 asks whether a tip should be calculated on the pre-tax or post-tax bill.

options.text: On zero, because tipping is optional.
On the post-tax amount, because tax raises the base.
On the tax only, because service is a tax.
On the pre-tax amount, since tax is not a service.

questions.explanation: Tip applies to the service cost before tax; the wrong idea inflates the base with tax.
questions.hint: Exclude tax from the tip base.

questions.stem: Ticket T-031 asks for the price per kilogram when 5 kg costs 12.50.

options.text: 0.40 per kilogram.
2.50 per kilogram.
62.50 per kilogram.
7.50 per kilogram.

questions.explanation: Divide 12.50 by 5 to get 2.50; the wrong steps invert, multiply, or subtract.

questions.stem: Ticket T-032 says leasing is always cheaper because monthly payments are lower than a purchase loan.

options.text: Buying is always cheaper because ownership has value.
Leasing is always cheaper because payments are lower.
Leasing may cost more over the full term once fees and residual are included.
Neither has cost because both are financed.

questions.explanation: Lower monthly payments can hide fees and residual charges; the error assumes lower payments mean lower total cost.

questions.stem: Ticket T-033 asks how to compute the penalty when paying off a loan early at 2 percent of the remaining balance of 5000.

answer.exemplar: Multiply the remaining balance by the penalty rate, giving 100; the wrong method applies the rate to the original principal or to the total interest.

questions.explanation: The penalty is a percentage of the remaining balance, giving 100; applying it to principal or interest is wrong.

questions.topic: Payment split into interest and principal
questions.learningObjective: Split a payment into interest and principal
questions.stem: Ticket T-034 splits a 200 payment on a 5000 balance at 1 percent monthly interest.
questions.explanation: Interest is 50, so principal is 150; the error treats the whole payment as principal.

questions.topic: Level deposit for a savings goal
questions.learningObjective: Compute level deposit for a goal
questions.stem: Ticket T-035 needs the annual deposit to reach 1000 in 2 years at 10 percent.
questions.explanation: The annuity payment formula gives about 476.19; the error divides 1000 by 2 and ignores interest.

questions.topic: Compound growth over a long horizon
questions.stem: Ticket T-036 asks why long horizons magnify the difference between simple and compound growth.

options.text: Neither grows because inflation cancels gains.
Simple growth accelerates because the rate rises.
Both grow at the same speed always.
Compound growth accelerates because interest earns interest.

questions.explanation: Compounding accelerates over time as interest earns interest; the wrong ideas assume linear growth or cancellation.

questions.topic: Percentage move in a share price
questions.stem: Ticket T-037 asks for the percentage change when a share moves from 80 to 100.

options.text: 20 percent.
25 percent.
100 percent.
80 percent.

questions.explanation: Change is 20 on a base of 80, so 25 percent; dividing by the new price gives 20 percent.

questions.topic: Currency conversion at a stated rate
questions.stem: Ticket T-038 converts 100 home currency at 1.25 foreign per home and gets 80.

options.text: 100 foreign is correct because rates are one to one.
125 foreign is correct because you multiply by the rate.
80 foreign is correct because you divide by the rate.
1 foreign is correct because you divide by 100.

questions.explanation: To get foreign currency divide home amount by foreign-per-home rate, giving 80; multiplying gives 125.

questions.topic: Real return from nominal and inflation
questions.stem: Ticket T-039 asks for the real return when nominal return is 7 percent and inflation is 3 percent.

answer.exemplar: Subtract inflation from nominal return to get about 4 percent; the wrong method adds the two percentages and overstates the real gain.

questions.explanation: Real return is nominal minus inflation, about 4 percent; adding the rates overstates the gain.

questions.stem: Ticket T-040 solves break-even for revenue 5x and cost 2x plus 30.
questions.explanation: Set 5x equal to 2x plus 30, giving 3x equals 30 and x equals 10; the error solves cost equals zero.

questions.topic: Simple interest compared with compound interest
questions.learningObjective: Compare simple and compound totals after two periods
questions.stem: Ticket T-041 computes the compound amount for 1000 at 5 percent for 2 years.
questions.explanation: 1000 times 1.05 squared is 1102.5; the error uses simple interest and gets 1100.

questions.stem: Ticket T-042 asks which expression gives the balance with monthly compounding.

options.text: P times (1 plus 12r) to the n.
P times (1 plus r) to the 12n.
P times (1 plus r over 12) to the n.
P times (1 plus r over 12) to the 12n.

questions.explanation: Monthly compounding divides the rate by 12 and multiplies periods by 12; the wrong forms misuse rate or periods.

questions.stem: Ticket T-043 asks for the margin when cost is 80 and selling price is 100.

options.text: 25 percent.
20 percent.
80 percent.
100 percent.

questions.explanation: Margin is profit over price, 20 over 100, so 20 percent; dividing by cost gives 25 percent markup.

questions.stem: Ticket T-044 says a tax-inclusive price of 108 and a tax-added price of 108 have the same pre-tax base.

options.text: The tax-added base is higher because tax is extra.
The bases are the same because both totals are 108.
The bases differ because one total already includes tax.
Neither has a base because tax is included.

questions.explanation: Equal totals do not imply equal bases when one includes tax; the tax-inclusive base is lower.
questions.hint: Remove tax from the inclusive total.

questions.stem: Ticket T-045 asks how to choose between 2 for 3.00 and 3 for 4.50.

answer.exemplar: Compute unit prices: 1.50 versus 1.50, so they are equal; the wrong method compares totals and picks the cheaper total.

questions.explanation: Both unit prices are 1.50, so neither is cheaper; comparing totals alone is misleading.

questions.topic: Annual percentage rate against note rate
questions.stem: Ticket T-046 has a note rate of 6 percent and fees that raise APR to 6.5 percent; find the extra annual cost on 1000.
questions.explanation: Extra cost is 1000 times 0.005, giving 5; the error multiplies by the full APR.

questions.stem: Ticket T-047 weights two stocks at 60 and 40 percent with returns 10 and 5 percent; find the index return.
questions.explanation: 0.6 times 10 plus 0.4 times 5 equals 8; the error averages the returns without weights.

questions.stem: Ticket T-048 asks for the exact real return when nominal is 10 percent and inflation is 4 percent.

options.text: 4 percent by using inflation only.
6 percent by subtracting 4 from 10.
14 percent by adding 10 and 4.
About 5.77 percent using (1.10/1.04)-1.

questions.explanation: Exact real return is (1.10/1.04)-1, about 5.77 percent; linear subtraction gives 6 percent.

questions.learningObjective: Find break-even from a quadratic cost
questions.stem: Ticket T-049 asks why a quadratic cost function may yield two break-even quantities.

options.text: Quadratics have no real solutions.
The parabola can cross the revenue line twice.
Revenue is always linear so no crossing occurs.
Cost is constant so one crossing only.

questions.explanation: A parabola can intersect a line in two points; the wrong ideas deny or misstate the shape.

questions.topic: Budget constraint and the affordable set
questions.stem: Ticket T-050 says a price increase for good X rotates the budget line outward.

options.text: A price increase shifts the budget line parallel outward.
A price increase rotates the budget line outward.
A price increase rotates the budget line inward, not outward.
Price changes do not affect the budget line.

questions.explanation: Higher price for X reduces affordable X, rotating inward; the error reverses or ignores the effect.

questions.topic: Minimum payment and a revolving balance
questions.stem: Ticket T-051 asks why making only minimum payments keeps a revolving balance high.

answer.exemplar: Minimum payments mostly cover interest, so principal declines slowly; the wrong idea assumes minimum payments clear the debt quickly.

questions.explanation: Small payments barely reduce principal, so interest keeps accruing; the error assumes rapid debt clearance.

questions.stem: Ticket T-052 compares saving 300 interest versus paying a 100 penalty; find the net benefit.
questions.explanation: Net benefit is 300 minus 100, giving 200; the error ignores the penalty.

questions.topic: Tax treatment of a retirement account
questions.stem: Ticket T-053 compares paying 20 percent tax now versus 25 percent later on 1000; find the better future value if invested at 0 percent growth.
questions.explanation: Paying 20 percent now leaves 800; deferring leaves 750, so paying now is better; the error compares rates without computing values.

questions.stem: Ticket T-054 applies a 20 percent discount then an extra 10 percent; find the final factor.

options.text: 0.90, keeping only the second discount.
0.70, adding the discounts.
0.80, keeping only the first discount.
0.72, multiplying 0.80 by 0.90.

questions.explanation: Successive discounts multiply: 0.80 times 0.90 equals 0.72; adding them is wrong.

questions.stem: Ticket T-055 asks what happens to import cost when the home currency weakens.

options.text: Import cost falls in home currency terms.
Import cost rises in home currency terms.
Import cost is unchanged because prices are fixed.
Import cost becomes zero because trade stops.

questions.explanation: A weaker home currency buys less foreign currency, raising import cost; the error reverses or ignores the effect.

questions.learningObjective: Compare purchasing power after two years
questions.stem: Ticket T-056 says purchasing power after two years of 4 percent inflation is 100 divided by 1.08.

options.text: The factor is 1 divided by 1.04.
The factor is 1 divided by 1.08.
options.misconception: uses simple inflation over two years

options.text: The correct factor is 1 divided by 1.04 squared.
The factor is 1.04 squared.

questions.explanation: Two years of inflation compound, so divide by 1.04 squared; 1.08 ignores compounding.

questions.learningObjective: Compute total amount with simple interest
questions.stem: Ticket T-057 asks for the total amount after simple interest on 1000 at 5 percent for 2 years.

answer.exemplar: Total amount equals principal plus interest, 1000 plus 100 equals 1100; the wrong method compounds and gets 1102.5.

questions.explanation: Simple interest adds 100 to 1000, giving 1100; compounding would give 1102.5 instead.

questions.topic: Solving for time under simple interest
questions.learningObjective: Solve for time with given values
questions.stem: Ticket T-058 solves for time when 100 interest accrues on 500 at 5 percent.
questions.explanation: Time equals 100 divided by (500 times 0.05), giving 4; the error divides by 0.05 only.

questions.stem: Ticket T-059 computes the compound amount for 2000 at 4 percent for 3 years.
questions.explanation: 2000 times 1.04 cubed is about 2249.73; the error uses simple interest and gets 2240.

questions.topic: Effective annual rate from monthly compounding
questions.stem: Ticket T-060 asks for the effective annual rate for 6 percent compounded monthly.

options.text: 72 percent, multiplying by 12.
6 percent, equating nominal and effective.
0.5 percent, using the monthly rate.
About 6.17 percent.

questions.explanation: EAR is (1+0.06/12)^12 minus 1, about 6.17 percent; the error equates nominal and effective.
